relevant_group_routes.relationship: Subaltern Studies essays treat peasant, tribal and worker action under colonial rule as politics with its own forms, and are criticised for overstating its autonomy (1982–88)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Sarkar (1997, pp. 86–87, read against the page images) lists early work that explored 'popular or subaltern autonomy in action, consciousness and culture': Hardiman on the peasant nationalists of Gujarat, Pandey on Congress organization and peasant militancy, Amin on rumours of Gandhi, studies of 'tribal movements and cults' and of Bengal labour. Bayly (1988; Verso reprint pp. 116–126, read) finds the essays' empirical work strong but holds that 'their concern to emphasize peasant autonomy seems to have deflected them from moving towards a “total history”' (p. 121) and that 'Simply to stress that autonomy ... is not very helpful in any attempt to specify the nature of historical change' (p. 126). O'Hanlon (1988; reprint pp. 85–86) criticises the 'literal interpretation of subaltern autonomy' in several contributions (Henningham, Ramachandra Guha, Dasgupta) while setting Ranajit Guha's book apart (p. 85). Ranajit Guha's own argument is the separate edge from his person entry.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: The programme statement of Subaltern Studies: a critique of colonialist and bourgeois-nationalist elitism, an autonomous but overlapping domain of 'the politics of the people', and a method of reading rebel consciousness through counter-insurgency records (1982–83)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Preface to Subaltern Studies I (dated Canberra, August 1981), read in the Selected Subaltern Studies reprint (Oxford, 1988), p. 35: the series is to 'rectify the elitist bias characteristic of much research and academic work' in South Asian studies; 'subaltern' is taken in the Concise Oxford sense, 'of inferior rank', as 'a name for the general attribute of subordination in South Asian society whether this is expressed in terms of class, caste, age, gender and office or in any other way'. 'On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India' (same reprint, pp. 37–44; Subaltern Studies I pagination is pp. 1–8): elitist historiography 'is of course not without its uses' (p. 38) but 'fails to acknowledge, far less interpret, the contribution made by the people on their own, that is, independently of the elite' (p. 39); 'What clearly is left out of this un-historical historiography is the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain, for it neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', 'As modern as indigenous elite politics' (p. 40); the two domains were not 'hermetically sealed off'; 'there was a great deal of overlap' (p. 42); the same class 'dominant in one area ... could be among the dominated in another' (p. 44). He claims a direction, not a doctrine: 'Let a hundred flowers blossom and we don't mind even the weeds' (p. 43); 'We claim no more than to try and indicate an orientation' (p. 43). Method, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983), introduction read (Duke 1999 printing, which keeps the 1983 Oxford pagination): 'To acknowledge the peasant as the maker of his own rebellion is to attribute ... a consciousness to him' (p. 4); 'How then are we to get in touch with the consciousness of insurgency when our access to it is barred thus by the discourse of counter-insurgency?'; 'It should be possible therefore to read the presence of a rebel consciousness as a necessary and pervasive element within that body of evidence' (p. 15). 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency', Subaltern Studies II (Delhi, 1983), pp. 1–42, read in full: historiography takes the peasant rebel 'merely as an empirical person or member of a class, but not as an entity whose will and reason constituted the praxis called rebellion' (p. 2); 'Cause is made to stand in as a phantom surrogate for Reason' (p. 3); the historian should 'stop pretending that it can fully grasp a past consciousness and reconstitute it' (p. 33). In-period reception, a member's reading first: Spivak, 'Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography', Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363 (read): the group 'offers a theory of change' (p. 330); its practice is 'closer to deconstruction' (p. 332) and its presuppositions are 'not, strictly speaking, consonant with a desire to find a consciousness (here of the subaltern) in a positive and pure state' (p. 333); quoting Elementary Aspects p. 15, she reads 'the project to retrieve the subaltern consciousness' 'as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest' (pp. 341–342), which 'would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness' (p. 356); 'The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women' but overlooks 'how important the concept-metaphor woman is' (p. 356). Rosalind O'Hanlon, 'Recovering the Subject' (Modern Asian Studies 22:1, 1988, pp. 189–224; read in the Verso reprint, 2000, pp. 72–115, whose pages are cited): 'the classic figure of Western humanism—the self-originating, self-determining individual ... is readmitted through the back door in the figure of the subaltern himself' (p. 74). C. A. Bayly, 'Rallying Around the Subaltern' (Journal of Peasant Studies 16:1, 1988, pp. 110–120; Verso reprint pp. 116–126): the Subalterns 'acted mainly as a catalyst' for an existing minority interest (p. 116); Guha's approach 'seems sometimes to postulate the existence of an unchanging peasantry and unified peasant consciousness defined by struggle with colonialism' (p. 121). Sumit Sarkar, 'The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies' (1997; pp. 82–87 and 90–94 read, pp. 84–87 against the page images): the early volumes were 'largely ignored in the West' while debated in 'Left-leaning intellectual circles in India' (p. 84); 'it was argued with considerable justice by Guha and other contributors' that anti-colonial movements had been explained 'far too often' by economic pressures and mobilization from the top (p. 85); the claims of a new 'paradigm' 'were certainly over-flamboyant' (p. 86); the theoretical turn 'had its origins in Guha's attempt to use some of the language and methods of Lévi-Straussian structuralism' (p. 87). Founder language is attributed, not adopted: Chakrabarty (1997) calls him 'the founder of the group' (subaltern source); Scott's foreword to the 1999 Duke printing writes that Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document of what is now known as the Subaltern Studies School', adding that 'The term school conveys far too much in the way of a rigid orthodoxy' (p. ix). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (Nepantla, 2000) treats 'the work of the historian Ranajit Guha in the period when he acted as the founding editor' as 'the founding texts of the project' (p. 11). edge_115 (subaltern → post) and edge_159 (gramsci → subaltern) stay.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Armitage credits Pagden with formative questions and continuing support for the doctoral study that developed into The Ideological Origins of the British Empire.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Armitage’s own acknowledgments p. x explicitly group Pagden with Chris Bayly, Peter Burke, Patrick Collinson and Istvan Hont in this Cambridge phase. All retain credit. This supports the named research contribution, not sole supervision, a particular question whose wording is unknown, or an inference from first meeting or institutional membership. Selected acknowledgments and publication leaves were read; Armitage’s full monograph remains unread.
